transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-21
Start: 15:00 PDT
End: 15:48 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Anita (CTO, ClearWave), Marcus (Eng Manager), Priya (SRE), Tom (Product), Speaker 6

Summary note (auto): weekly POC sync — focus on TTFT (time-to-first-token) spikes around microbursts and streaming handshake variance; discuss kernel choices for short vs long sequence workloads; decide on hedging playbook.

[00:00] Samira (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we've got 45-ish minutes on the calendar. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Anita (ClearWave): Anita here.
[00:09] Marcus: Marcus, yep.
[00:11] Priya: Priya on SRE.
[00:13] Tom: Tom from product.
[00:15] Diego (Redwood SE): Diego here.
[00:17] Samira: Great. Quick agenda — Diego will walk through the post-run microburst profiles, we talk hedging options, kernel choices for short seqlen, and pick next steps. Sound good?

[00:30] Diego: Cool. I'm gonna share my screen — lemme know if the spreadsheet link didn't land, Samira?
[00:35] Samira: Link's in the chat, yep.

[01:05] Diego: Alright, so what we saw in the last run — and this is on the staging Dedicated pool — was a TTFT regression centered at microburst 95th/99th percentiles when we hit a flood of 40–80 token requests. The average token latency is fine but the first token saw spikes up to 420ms where baseline is usually 160–220ms. That's with streaming enabled and our default kernel selection.

[01:45] Marcus: Is that repeatable on hosted or only on Dedicated?
[01:50] Diego: We reproduced it on dedicated and a smaller repro on hosted; hosted masks some spikes because of different batching heuristics but we're seeing the pattern.

[02:10] Anita: Where do you think the time is being spent — scheduler, kernel warmup, KV cache cold start?

[02:18] Diego: Good q. The flame graphs we collected point to two things: kernel dispatching for short sequences becomes non-trivial when the runtime switches kernels mid-network, and KV cache warmup for repeated chat prefixes. The streaming handshake also adds ~30–60ms variance due to the initial chunk framing.

[02:42] Tom: When you say kernel switch, is that the CUDA kernel choice or the micro-optimized path for 8-bit quantized models?

[02:52] Diego: Both, kind of. We have a 'fast-small' kernel for short seqlen that uses fused attention; another path uses a more general but slightly heavier kernel for longer seqlens. When requests vary, the runtime may flip which kernel or execution path to use and that flip causes a short scheduling hiccup. On top of that, if KV cache isn't warm, the first request will pay the penalty.

[03:28] Priya: We're mostly short requests — typical chat user 12–45 tokens. So this is in our critical path.

[03:35] Samira: Okay, so the ask for this week is — can we pick a hedging/playbook approach? Options are: 1) force fast-small kernel for seqlen <= 64 (static override), 2) keep dynamic kernel selection but add a micro-hedge (duplicate small fraction of requests to alternate kernel until warm), 3) tweak streaming framing to reduce handshake variance.

[04:02] Marcus: Option 1 sounds simplest but worried about accuracy/cost tradeoffs if the small kernel is less precise on some prompts.

[04:12] Diego: Right — in our lab tests the small kernel had negligible quality diff on 90% of prompts, but for the long-tail prompts with math or long context it degrades completion length slightly. We can set a conservative threshold or a content-marker to switch.

[04:35] Anita: How about option 2 — hedging — sounds like it might add cost but reduces tail. How much overhead?

[04:43] Diego: If we hedge 5–10% of requests to an alternate path during warmup windows, cost goes up by roughly that percent but TTFT tail drops dramatically in our sims. We can implement adaptive hedging so it's only active when the runtime detects seqlen churn or microburst patterns.

[05:05] Samira: Diego, are there any auto-thresholds we can expose to ClearWave so your SRE can tune without redeploy?

[05:12] Diego: Yep — we can expose seqlen cutoff, hedging rate, and streaming chunk size as runtime flags in the Dedicated config. For Private/VPC we can surface them in the control plane; for on-prem we'd provide a config file.

[05:30] Speaker 6: (inaudible) — sorry lost a chunk.

[06:05] Diego: Back to the data — I put two tabs in the sheet: 'microburst-run-09-20' and 'kv-warmup-09-20'. The microburst run shows a correlated spike with bursts of concurrent short requests; the KV tab shows that after ~7 repeated prefixes the cache hit rate stabilizes and TTFT returns to baseline. So if you can keep some prefix reuse or preload cache, that helps.

[06:45] Priya: Preloading cache — that requires stateful session reuse, right? We can do that from the client side but not trivial with our mobile users.

[06:54] Diego: Correct — session affinity helps. We also have an automated prefix predictor that can prefetch common KV keys based on user id; that's part of Redwood Optimize recommendations but it's more involved. For the POC we recommend two simpler tactics: 1) increase short-lived session affinity window to 30s, 2) run cache warmup for known hot prefixes during onboarding flows.

[07:22] Tom: Can we detect microbursts at the API gateway and enable hedging dynamically?

[07:30] Diego: Yes, our routing layer supports threshold-based policies. We can roll a canary that flips hedging on when qps/sec > X for short-seqlen class. But it needs careful tuning to avoid extra cost during normal surges.

[07:50] Marcus: How about streaming framing — you mentioned it adds 30–60ms variance, what's the tweak?

[07:56] Diego: Two levers: reduce initial chunk size (more but smaller frames) or change the handshake to inline first chunk with request so you avoid a separate ack step. The latter requires client-side change or SDK update; the former is runtime-configurable.

[08:20] Anita: SDK changes will be tough for our product this week. Prefer runtime knobs.

[08:28] Diego: Then we recommend changing initial chunk size and enabling fast-small kernel override for seqlen <= 48 as a baseline.

[08:40] Samira: Let's pause for objections. Any blockers to trying that today?

[08:45] Priya: The only blocker is we need a formal change request for our staging VPC to alter session affinity policies. Anita will approve but we need to log the change.

[08:56] Anita: Yep, will do.

[09:02] Diego: I'll package the commands and the script; it'll be a one-line config flip in the Dedicated control plane and an env var for private.

[09:20] Marcus: One question — does forcing the fast kernel reduce our throughput for longer requests? If we misclassify, will we blow up CPU/GPU time?

[09:30] Diego: It can slightly increase token compute if the kernel is not ideal for that sequence length, but for your workload — mostly short — the overall cost per token is about the same or slightly lower. For long requests it could be 3–6% slower; that's why we want an adaptive threshold.

[09:55] Tom: Any visibility in Redwood Console to see when the kernel switch happens?

[10:00] Diego: Yes, we already surface per-request kernel metrics in the console and you can trace by token. We'll add a per-route view so you can see the % hedged, kernel choices, and TTFT heatmap.

[10:18] Samira: Quick practical: Diego, can you run two short microbenchmarks and post results — one with current dynamic kernel and streaming default, one with forced fast-small kernel and reduced chunk size?

[10:27] Diego: Yep. I was planning to run three actually: dynamic baseline, forced-fast kernel, and adaptive hedging at 10% for 15 minutes. I'll upload CSVs.

[10:38] Anita: If we see the hedging win but cost increases by 8–10%, we'll need numbers to propose to finance.

[10:45] Samira: I'll produce the cost delta and a note about conversion uplift expectations — sometimes reducing TTFT increases engagement a bit, so ROI isn't purely token-cost.

[11:00] Marcus: Curious whether Anthropic or Vertex have similar hedging features; might be relevant for procurement.

[11:06] Samira: Some vendors have request duplication features but they tend to be wholesale and not kernel-aware. We'll include a short competitive note in the email.

[11:18] Diego: One more datapoint — we observed that the first-token spike often correlates with garbage collection on the host when memory churn is high. We're going to instrument GC pauses and GPU mem copies on the next run. Might be another angle.

[11:35] Priya: If GC is part of it, maybe moving to a slightly higher reserved GPU memory partition helps?

[11:42] Diego: Could — we can tweak allocation strategies. That gets into infra tuning which we can do with you in a later deep dive.

[12:00] Samira: Ok, let's capture next steps. Diego — microbenchmarks + CSV + short notes by 09-24. ClearWave (Anita/Priya) — run staging scenario 500 concurrent short requests, share logs by 09-25. Samira — pricing and microburst SLA draft by 09-27.

[12:20] Anita: All good. Also can you add a short security note — any implications of hedging on PII or logs?

[12:28] Diego: Hedged requests are internal duplicates and we keep them in the same tenancy, so no additional external surface. Logging is the same; we can redact or not persist duplicates depending on policy.

[12:40] Tom: One last product ask — can we get a recommended default playbook writeup? Like a one-pager for eng explaining when to flip to forced kernel vs hedging?

[12:48] Diego: Yes — I'll hand off a playbook doc and a set of CLI commands. Samira will include that in the follow-up email.

[13:05] Speaker 6: (background) — quick thought — what about prewarm instances?

[13:10] Samira: Pre-warm is possible via reserve burst pools; that's effectively Dedicated burst capacity which we can price. We'll include that option.

[13:22] Anita: If prewarm cost is lower than hedging costs in production, that might be preferable. We'll want numbers.

[13:30] Diego: I'll add a cost-comparison row in the spreadsheet: hedging vs prewarm vs forced kernel.

[13:45] Marcus: Great. Anything else?

[13:50] Priya: Minor — can you ensure the CSV includes the full request trace id so we can join with our gateway logs?

[13:58] Diego: Yep will include request IDs and kernel tag per request.

[14:10] Samira: Ok, wrap. We'll send meeting notes, attach the sheet, the playbook draft, and suggested control-plane flips. Follow-up meeting next week same time to go over results — should we do Tue 09-29?

[14:22] Anita: Tue works.

[14:25] Samira: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[14:28] Diego: Thanks.
[14:30] Meeting end.
